title: Media, body image and self-esteem
keyIdea: Most images of bodies in ads and on social media are picked from many shots, then posed, lit, smoothed, reshaped or filtered. Edits leave clues, like straight lines that bend near a body or skin with no texture. Comparing yourself with these images is upward comparison: your everyday life against someone else's edited best moments. That tends to lower body image and mood, and labels saying an image was retouched do little to stop it. What helps is naming the comparison, reframing the thought, valuing what your body can do (body functionality), and curating your feed and your time on it. If worries about your body take over, talk to a trusted adult or your GP.
familyTip: Next time you scroll together, play spot the edit: look for bent door frames, smooth skin and perfect light. Talk about what people choose not to post. Ask which accounts leave you feeling better or worse, and mute one that makes you feel worse.

visual.caption: Does this habit help or harm body image? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Mute accounts that make you feel worse
Edit every selfie before you post
Zoom in on your photos to find flaws
Thank your body for what it can do
Count likes to judge how you look

lab.caption: Flagship lab: edit a photo the way posted images are made, spot the clues, sort a highlight reel, reframe comparison thoughts, and sort habits that help.

kid: Most photos of bodies you see online are not one quick snap. People take lots of shots and post the best one. Then they may change the light, the angle, the skin or the shape. Some apps add a filter as you take the photo. So the person in the photo does not look like that in real life.
Edits leave clues. A door frame or a floor line may bend near the body. Skin may have no pores or marks at all. Real skin always has some texture.

When you compare yourself with someone who seems better off, that is called upward comparison. Online, you set your normal day against their best and edited moments. That is not a fair test. It often makes people feel worse about how they look.

Self-esteem is how you value yourself overall. You can protect it. Notice when you are comparing, and name it. Think about what your body can do, not just how it looks. Mute accounts that make you feel bad, and take breaks. If worries about your body take over, tell a trusted adult or your GP.
adult: Ages 14 to 15. In England this is part of PSHE at key stage 4: self-concept, and how media and social media affect body image. The DfE guidance for health education (2019) also asks that pupils learn how online images can be changed, and how comparing ourselves with others affects how we feel.

The evidence points one way. People judge themselves by comparing with others (Festinger, 1954). Fardouly and colleagues found that more time on photo apps, and more comparing with people who look better, goes with worse body image. Kleemans and colleagues (2018) showed teenage girls edited photos. The girls thought the photos were real, and felt worse after. In a 2023 trial by Thai and colleagues, young people cut social media to one hour a day for three weeks. They then felt better about their looks and weight.

A common mistake is to think a label fixes it. Tiggemann and colleagues found that notes like this image has been edited did little to help. Another mistake is to tell teenagers to just ignore the images. It works better to name the comparison and reframe the thought. In trials, focusing on what the body can do, not how it looks, has improved body image (Alleva and colleagues, 2015).

In the lab the learner turns on six edits: best of 30 shots, light, angle, smoothing, reshaping and a face filter. They find the clue in three edited photos and sort seven moments into posted or not posted. Then they pick fairer replies to three comparison thoughts and sort six habits. If body worries affect eating, sleep or mood, see a GP. In the UK, the charity Beat helps young people with eating worries.

practice.prompt: Which is a clue that a photo was reshaped?
choices: A door frame bends near the body
The person is smiling
The photo was taken outside
practice.hint: Look at straight lines behind the person.
practice.explain: A warp tool pulls in a waist or leg and drags the background with it, so straight lines curve near the body.

practice.prompt: An influencer takes {a} selfies and posts 1. How many shots did you never see?
practice.hint: Take away the one that was posted.
practice.explain: {a} − 1 = {=a-1} shots stayed off the feed. You only saw the best one.

practice.prompt: You feel worse after scrolling past fitness posts. What is going on?
choices: Upward comparison with edited best moments
Your body is the problem
The posts show how most people look
practice.hint: Who are you comparing yourself with, and what kind of photos are they?
practice.explain: You are comparing your everyday self with other people's picked and edited best shots. That upward comparison tends to lower mood.

practice.prompt: You use social media for {a} hours a day. If you cut it to 1 hour a day, how many hours do you free up in a week?
practice.hint: Work out the hours saved each day, then multiply by 7.
practice.explain: You save {=a-1} hours a day, and {=a-1} × 7 = {=7*(a-1)} hours a week.

practice.prompt: Which thought focuses on body functionality?
choices: My legs carried me up that hill
My legs should look thinner
My legs look fine in this filter
practice.hint: Functionality is about what your body does.
practice.explain: Valuing what your body can do, like walking up a hill, moves attention away from how it looks.

choices: Comparing yourself with people who seem better off
Comparing yourself with people who seem worse off
Asking a role model for advice
pool.hint: Up means towards people who seem to have more.
pool.explain: Upward comparison means measuring yourself against people who seem better off. With edited images it tends to lower mood and body image.

pool.prompt: An ad says the image has been retouched. What do studies find about labels like this?
choices: They do little to stop people feeling worse
They make the image harmless
They make viewers like their own bodies more
pool.hint: Think about whether knowing changes how an image makes you feel.
pool.explain: Studies by Tiggemann and colleagues found retouching labels did little to reduce body dissatisfaction.

pool.prompt: A face in a photo has no pores, lines or marks at all. What does that suggest?
choices: Skin smoothing or a filter was used
The person has perfect skin
The camera was very good
pool.hint: Does any real skin have no texture?
pool.explain: All real skin has texture. A face with none has almost always been smoothed or filtered.

pool.prompt: Out of {a} photos on a feed, {b} were edited. How many were not edited?
pool.hint: Take the edited photos away from the total.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} photos were not edited, and you often cannot tell which ones they are.

pool.prompt: In a trial, young people cut social media to 1 hour a day for 3 weeks. Someone who usually uses {a} hours a day would cut how many hours in total?
pool.hint: Hours saved each day, times 21 days.
pool.explain: They save {=a-1} hours a day for 21 days: {=a-1} × 21 = {=21*(a-1)} hours.

pool.prompt: Your friend says everyone will notice the spot on her chin. What is a fair reply?
choices: People notice us far less than we think
Filter it out before anyone sees
Stay home until it is gone
pool.explain: The spotlight effect means we think others notice us much more than they do. Hiding or filtering keeps the worry going.

pool.prompt: Which habit is most likely to protect body image?
choices: Muting accounts that make you feel worse
Editing every selfie before posting
Counting likes to judge your looks
pool.explain: Muting accounts that trigger comparison means fewer edited bodies in your feed. Heavy editing and like counting tie worth to looks.

choices: How you value yourself overall
How you look in photos
How many likes you get
pool.hint: It is wider than looks or numbers on an app.
pool.explain: Self-esteem is your overall sense of your own worth. Looks are only one part, and likes depend on timing and the app.

pool.prompt: Worries about your body start to affect your eating and sleep. What should you do?
choices: Talk to a trusted adult or your GP
Keep it to yourself
Follow more fitness influencers
pool.hint: Who can help you get support?
pool.explain: When body worries affect eating, sleep or mood, getting help early matters. A trusted adult or GP can help; in the UK, Beat supports young people too.
